screens.title: First Hop Redundancy Protocols
screens.narratorSegment: In enterprise networks, the default gateway is the first hop every host uses to reach destinations outside its subnet. If that gateway device fails, many users instantly lose connectivity. This lesson introduces first hop redundancy protocols, or FHRPs, which present a virtual IP and virtual MAC so hosts can keep sending traffic even if a physical router goes offline. We'll focus on Cisco's HSRP and GLBP, and the open-standard VRRP. You'll learn the difference between active versus standby roles, how virtual MACs enable seamless failover, and when true load balancing with GLBP is preferable to simple redundancy. We'll also cover operational controls like preemption, priority, tracking, and authentication so your redundancy behaves predictably and securely. For example, with HSRP you can let the highest-priority switch be active, but use tracking to lower its priority if an uplink fails so traffic doesn't get blackholed. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to configure and verify HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP on Layer 3 switches and interpret their states with show commands. Consider how your campus or data center could benefit when a single device failure no longer disrupts user traffic.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › First Hop Redundancy Protocols
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

First Hop Redundancy Protocols

Learn how HSRP, VRRP and GLBP present a single virtual gateway to hosts so traffic keeps flowing during a router outage. Understand roles, failover, and when to use each protocol.

In this lesson
Gateway redundancy, HSRP basics, GLBP load distribution
Coming up
Configuration examples, tracking and authentication
Hands-on
CLI starter code for SW1 and SW2 with verification commands
Explore Key Topics
FHRP Purpose
Why virtual IP/MAC prevents a single-device outage from disconnecting hosts.
HSRP & VRRP
Active/Standby vs Master/Backup roles and cross-vendor considerations.
GLBP
True per-packet load balancing using AVG/AVF and virtual MAC assignment.
Visual Concept
Virtual gateway identity shared by multiple routers
Virtual IP
A single IP responded to by the FHRP group so hosts use one gateway address.
Virtual MAC
A shared MAC used to forward frames; GLBP assigns multiple virtual MACs for load sharing.
Why this matters
Virtual identities decouple host gateway configuration from any single physical device. This simplifies failover and supports maintenance without mass reconfiguration of endpoints.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will understand why FHRPs are essential and how to operate three protocols used for first-hop resilience. First, you will be able to explain the necessity of a virtual IP and virtual MAC in preventing a single point of failure and give an example where an access switch host keeps routing during a gateway failure. Second, you will configure and verify HSRP for active/standby use, and create multiple HSRP groups for basic load distribution; this matters because many campus designs use HSRP on Layer 3 switches for VLAN gateways. Third, you will configure VRRP as the open-standard alternative and describe where VRRP’s behavior differs from HSRP; this is important in multi-vendor environments. Fourth, you will set up GLBP to deliver true per-packet or per-host load balancing using AVG and AVF roles, and use tracking and authentication to make failover graceful and secure. Each objective includes practical commands and verification so you can apply the skills in a lab or production environment.

screens.title: What are FHRPs and how virtual IP/MAC works
screens.narratorSegment: First hop redundancy protocols create a shared gateway identity that hosts use as their default route. The shared identity consists of a virtual IP and usually a virtual MAC. Hosts ARP for the default gateway IP and receive a single MAC that corresponds to the protocol's virtual address. The key benefit is that host configurations remain static; endpoints do not need to know which physical router is active, and traffic continues to flow if a router fails. For example, an office workstation pointing at 192.168.10.1 continues to reach the internet when the physical switch that was forwarding traffic goes offline because a standby router assumes the virtual identity. A common misconception is that FHRPs make the network magically multipath; they provide gateway availability and, in GLBP's case, load distribution, but they do not replace proper bandwidth planning. Another point is that the virtual MAC is the control point for forwarding: if the MAC maps to a new physical device, frames follow. Remember that while HSRP and VRRP present a single virtual MAC for the group, GLBP assigns multiple virtual MACs so different hosts map to different physical forwarders. Think about how ARP caching on hosts and switch CAM behavior will affect failover timing and transient forwarding. How would you explain this behavior to an endpoint team concerned about ARP cache timeouts?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An FHRP shares a virtual IP and MAC so hosts keep a consistent gateway even when physical devices fail.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › FHRP Definition
Core Concept

Virtual IP and MAC explained

An FHRP presents a virtual gateway identity so hosts send traffic without needing to change their configuration when a physical router fails.

How ARP is used
Hosts ARP for the virtual IP and store the returned virtual MAC. When failover occurs, subsequent ARP or refreshed entries point to the new forwarder.
Misconception
FHRPs provide availability; they do not automatically multiply bandwidth unless GLBP is used to distribute hosts across forwarders.
Concrete Example
Workstation uses 192.168.10.1 as gateway. SW1 is active. SW1 fails. Standby becomes active and replies for 192.168.10.1 with the same virtual MAC so the workstation keeps sending traffic.
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Virtual identities keep host configurations static and enable seamless gateway failover when routers change roles.

screens.title: HSRP fundamentals — Active, Standby, and Listen
screens.narratorSegment: HSRP is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that elects one router to be Active and another to be Standby while the remaining routers listen. The Active router forwards traffic sent to the virtual IP and responds to ARP requests for the virtual MAC. Standby monitors the Active router using hello messages and will take over if the Active stops sending them. Other routers remain in the Listen state and do not forward for the virtual gateway. Election uses configured priority values; the highest priority becomes Active. If priorities match, the router with the higher IP address wins. Configuration typically uses standby group commands on the interface level to set the virtual IP, priority, and optionally enable preemption. A common pitfall is forgetting preempt: if a higher-priority router reboots and comes back online, without preempt it will not reclaim Active status and the network may continue using the lower-priority forwarder. Another practical consideration is ARP cache timing—after failover, host ARP entries may still reference an earlier MAC until they expire or refresh. In designs that require load sharing across VLANs, multiple HSRP groups can be used so different routers are Active for different subnets. Think about how you'll combine HSRP groups and tracking so a router with a failed uplink loses Active status for all relevant groups.

keyIdea.title: HSRP Roles
keyIdea.text: Active forwards, Standby waits to take over, and Listen routers observe — priority and preempt control elections.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › HSRP Fundamentals
Core Concept

HSRP role election and behavior

HSRP elects an Active router to forward traffic for a virtual IP. Standby waits to assume the role if the Active fails. Listeners remain passive.

Election mechanics
Highest priority becomes Active. Matching priorities tie-break with higher IP. Preempt allows higher-priority routers to reclaim Active after recovery.
Common mistake
Forgetting preempt can leave a higher-capability router in standby after it reboots, changing capacity unexpectedly.
Example Scenario
SW1 priority 150 is Active for VLAN 10. SW2 priority 100 is Standby. SW1 uplink fails; SW2 takes Active. When SW1 uplink returns, with preempt enabled and no tracking decrement, SW1 reclaims Active.
Check your understanding
What happens if both routers have equal priority and the same IP is misconfigured? Election will use the highest IP tie-breaker, so consistent IP configuration matters.

screens.title: Configuring HSRP — commands and verification
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through configuring HSRP on a VLAN interface and how to verify its operation. On an interface you define the virtual IP with standby group commands, set a priority, and enable preemption if you want a higher-priority device to reclaim Active after it recovers. For instance, setting standby 1 ip 192.168.10.1 and standby 1 priority 150 on SW1 configures the group. You also enable standby 1 preempt so SW1 will become Active again after reboot. To verify, run show standby brief to view the group's Active state, Virtual IP, and active MAC. A useful troubleshooting step is to purposely shut an uplink and confirm the standby becomes active, then bring the uplink back and ensure preemption behaves as expected. One misconception to avoid is believing that preempt alone guarantees immediate takeover; tracking can lower effective priority so preempt will not take effect if the calculated priority is lower. When you configure HSRP at scale, document group numbers per VLAN so you can plan load distribution. Practice these commands in the lab and use show standby and interface status to correlate physical and logical states.

keyIdea.text: Use standby <group> ip, priority, and preempt; verify with show standby brief and test failover under controlled conditions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › HSRP Configuration
Config Example
configure terminal
hostname SW1
!
interface Vlan10
 ip address 192.168.10.10 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 192.168.10.1
 standby 1 priority 150
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet1/0/24 decrement 60
!
end
This snippet shows the key commands: define virtual IP, set priority, enable preemption, and track an uplink to adjust priority dynamically.
Verification
show standby brief — lists groups, roles, virtual IPs, and active MACs.
show interface Vlan10 — check interface and IP alignment with HSRP group.
Use debug standby only in a lab to observe hello messages and election events.
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Practical CLI configuration plus verification commands will reveal group state and help you test failover safely.

screens.title: HSRP preemption, priority, and tracking
screens.narratorSegment: Controlling who becomes Active is essential for predictable forwarding. Priority values determine election: higher priority wins. Preemption is a flag that permits a device with a higher priority, once it recovers, to take back the Active role. Tracking lets you tie effective priority to the state of an interface or object. For example, you can configure standby 1 track GigabitEthernet1/0/24 decrement 60. If that uplink goes down, the router reduces its effective priority by 60. If the resulting effective priority falls below the standby partner, the partner will become Active. Tracking avoids a situation where a router with a failed upstream path remains Active and blackholes traffic. A common misconception is thinking preempt overrides tracking; it does not. If a tracked interface remains down, the calculated priority might be lower so the higher-priority router will not preempt. In practice, plan your decrement values carefully so that a tracked failure reliably forces failover, but temporary blips don’t cause oscillation. Test by bringing the tracked interface down and observing show standby brief to confirm how the effective priority changed and which router became Active.

keyIdea.title: Control mechanisms
keyIdea.text: Use priority, preempt, and track together so a recovered router only reclaims Active when its path and services are healthy.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Preempt & Tracking
Process

Priority → Preempt → Tracking

Step 1: Assign priorities so the most capable device has the highest value.
Step 2: Enable preempt on devices that should reclaim Active when healthy.
Step 3: Track critical uplinks or services and decrement priority when they fail to force failover.
Example
standby 1 priority 150 standby 1 preempt standby 1 track GigabitEthernet1/0/24 decrement 60 If the tracked uplink fails, effective priority is 90, and a standby partner with priority 100 becomes Active.
Misconception check
Preempt will not force a takeover if the recovered router's calculated priority after tracking is lower than the current Active. Trackings can stop preemption from causing flaps.

screens.title: VRRP — open-standard alternative to HSRP
screens.narratorSegment: VRRP is the open-standard counterpart to HSRP and maps closely to the same concepts: a Master router forwards traffic for a virtual IP while Backup routers monitor and take over if the Master fails. Configuration uses vrrp group commands to set the virtual IP, priority, and optionally preempt. A key difference is that VRRP allows the virtual IP to be the actual IP address of the Master interface in some configurations, simplifying address management in mixed-vendor environments. Because VRRP is standardized in RFC 5798, it’s preferred when routers from different vendors must participate in gateway redundancy. Operationally, hello and hold timers work the same way in principle, and tracking and authentication are available similarly. An important misconception to avoid is assuming VRRP and HSRP are interchangeable without attention to subtle defaults like timers and authentication commands; when mixing vendors, confirm those settings match. When designing redundancy, choose VRRP when you need cross-vendor support and HSRP when you require Cisco-specific features or operational familiarity. Always verify with show vrrp brief to confirm Master selection and virtual MAC assignment. VRRP — open-standard alternative to HSRP means vrrp provides master/backup redundancy like hsrp but as an open standard suited for multi-vendor deployments.. In practical terms, how vrrp maps to hsrp roles and a key configuration difference. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › VRRP Overview
Comparison

VRRP vs HSRP

Both provide a virtual IP and election. HSRP uses Active/Standby terminology; VRRP uses Master/Backup.
VRRP is standardized and often easier for mixed-vendor setups; HSRP is Cisco-proprietary with long operational familiarity in Cisco shops.
Be careful with default timers and authentication settings when mixing protocols across vendors.
Example
vrrp 1 ip 192.168.10.1 vrrp 1 priority 110 vrrp 1 preempt This mirrors HSRP but uses vrrp commands and is vendor-neutral.
Verification
show vrrp brief — confirm Master and Backup states, priorities, and virtual IP ownership.

screens.title: GLBP architecture — AVG and AVF roles
screens.narratorSegment: GLBP differs from HSRP and VRRP by allowing multiple physical routers to actively forward traffic for the same virtual IP. The protocol elects an Active Virtual Gateway, or AVG, which assigns unique virtual MACs to each Active Virtual Forwarder, or AVF. When a host ARPs for the virtual IP, the AVG replies with one of the AVF's virtual MAC addresses, often in round-robin order. That causes different hosts to have different MAC-to-physical-router mappings and distributes the forwarding load. GLBP supports multiple load-balancing methods: round-robin, host-dependent, and weighted. Round-robin cycles ARP responses among AVFs. Weighted allows AVFs to receive ARP responses proportional to their weight, useful if routers have asymmetric capacity. One misconception is assuming GLBP provides per-packet distribution; GLBP's distribution happens at ARP resolution time, so flows from the same host usually stick to a single AVF. When designing with GLBP, set priorities and weights thoughtfully and use show glbp brief to verify AVG, AVF roles, and virtual MAC assignments. GLBP is well-suited for environments where you want all gateway devices to share forwarding load without configuring multiple groups per VLAN.

keyIdea.title: GLBP takeaway
keyIdea.text: GLBP uses an AVG to assign virtual MACs to AVFs so multiple routers can forward for the same virtual IP, enabling load sharing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › GLBP Architecture
Architecture

AVG and AVF roles

AVG assigns virtual MACs and responds to ARP for the virtual IP using a load-balancing algorithm.
AVFs are the routers that forward traffic for their assigned virtual MACs.
Distribution occurs at ARP resolution; hosts typically stick to the AVF they learned, preserving flow affinity.
Concrete Example
GLBP group 20 with SW1 as AVG assigns MAC A to SW1 and MAC B to SW2. When clients ARP, some receive MAC A and others MAC B. The effect is parallel gateway usage for the same virtual IP.
Verification
show glbp brief — confirms AVG, AVFs, virtual MACs and weights so you can verify distribution.

screens.title: Configuring GLBP and load-balancing methods
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring GLBP starts with defining the GLBP group and virtual IP on the interface using glbp ip. Next set priorities and preemption as needed and choose a load-balancing method: round-robin, host-dependent, or weighted. Round-robin rotates ARP responses among AVFs and is the simplest default. Weighted lets you assign relative weights so higher-capacity routers receive ARP responses more often. For example, glbp 20 load-balancing round-robin configures the default behavior. Verification uses show glbp brief to confirm which router is AVG, which are AVFs, and the virtual MAC addresses assigned. Keep in mind GLBP gives per-host distribution at ARP resolution; it does not change the fact that each host typically sends all its traffic to one AVF until ARP changes. A common design choice is to use GLBP in VLANs where many hosts need to be balanced across distribution switches for capacity reasons. Avoid expecting instantaneous rebalancing when a device goes down—GLBP relies on ARP and may require ARP refresh to move hosts to remaining AVFs. Practice with different weights in the lab and observe how show glbp brief reports assignments. Configuring GLBP and load-balancing methods means use glbp <group> ip <virtual-ip>, set load-balancing to round-robin or weighted, and verify roles and macs with show glbp brief.. In practical terms, commands, weights, and when to use round-robin vs weighted. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Configuring GLBP starts with defining the GLBP group and virtual IP on the interface using glbp ip. Next set priorities and preemption as needed and choose a load-balancing method: round-robin, host-dependent, or weighted. Round-robin rotates ARP responses among AVFs and is the simplest default. Weighted lets you assign relative weights so higher-capacity routers receive ARP responses more often. For example, glbp 20 load-balancing round-robin configures the default behavior. Verification uses show glbp brief to confirm which router is AVG, which are AVFs, and the virtual MAC addresses assigned. Keep in mind GLBP gives per-host distribution at ARP resolution; it does not change the fact that each host typically sends all its traffic to one AVF until ARP changes. A common design choice is to use GLBP in VLANs where many hosts need to be balanced across distribution switches for capacity reasons. Avoid expecting instantaneous rebalancing when a device goes down—GLBP relies on ARP and may require ARP refresh to move hosts to remaining AVFs. Practice with different weights in the lab and observe how show glbp brief reports assignments. Configuring GLBP and load-balancing methods means use glbp <group> ip <virtual-ip>, set load-balancing to round-robin or weighted, and verify roles and macs with show glbp brief.. screens.title: Tracking and authentication across FHRPs
screens.narratorSegment: Tracking and authentication are essential operational features for reliable and secure FHRP behavior. Tracking lets a router reduce its effective priority when a monitored object, typically an interface, goes down. You configure tracking with standby track [decrement ] for HSRP or vrrp track [decrement ] for VRRP and GLBP tracking syntax. The tracked decrement ensures that a router with a failed uplink does not become or remain Active, preventing traffic black-holing. Authentication prevents unauthorized devices from joining and impersonating the virtual gateway. For HSRP, you can configure MD5 authentication using standby authentication md5 key-string. Authentication prevents rogue devices from taking over by validating hellos. A common operational mistake is mismatched authentication parameters between peers, which prevents group formation. Another is setting too-large decrements that force unnecessary failovers for short-lived glitches. In your designs, balance sensitivity with stability: pick decrements that reflect real service loss and match authentication across peers. Regularly verify tracked objects and test the behavior in a lab before deploying to production. Tracking and authentication across FHRPs means use tracking to make failover decisions reflect upstream health and authentication to block rogue participants.. In practical terms, protecting failover decisions and securing group membership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Troubleshooting FHRPs — show and debug tactics
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting FHRPs requires careful observation of show command output and conservative use of debug. Start with show standby brief, show vrrp brief, and show glbp brief to inspect group numbers, roles, effective priorities, virtual IPs, and virtual MACs. Compare these outputs across peers to confirm consistent virtual IP usage and matching authentication. If a group fails to form, look for mismatched timers, authentication keys, or incorrect interface bindings. Use interface show commands to verify IP addresses and whether the interface is up. If further detail is necessary, use debug standby or debug vrrp sparingly in a lab or maintenance window, because debug can affect device performance. Observing hellos can reveal why a router is not receiving or not sending messages. For GLBP-specific troubleshooting, confirm the AVG and AVF assignments and check weights when using weighted mode. A common root cause is an uplink or route problem, not the FHRP itself; tracking is intended to mitigate that risk by lowering priority when upstream paths fail. When diagnosing, correlate control-plane messages with data-plane symptoms and avoid making configuration changes blindly—document the current state, test in a lab, and then apply fixes during a maintenance window when possible.

screens.title: Design patterns and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When deploying FHRPs across a campus or data center, follow a few practical patterns to ensure stability and predictability. Use clear group numbering conventions per VLAN so you can plan which device is Active for which subnet without guesswork. For HSRP, assign higher priorities to devices with stronger uplinks and enable preempt only when you are confident tracked objects reflect production readiness. Use tracking to cause a router to step down when its upstream path fails. For GLBP, pick load-balancing methods that match application behavior: round-robin for broad distribution, weighted when routers have different capacity, and host-dependent when session affinity matters. Avoid overusing multiple groups across many VLANs to simulate load balancing; GLBP can be simpler where supported. Common mistakes include mismatched authentication, forgetting preempt where expected, inappropriate decrement magnitudes causing flapping, and assuming immediate rebalancing when an AVF fails. Document your configuration, test failover in a lab, and monitor after rollouts. Ask yourself: have I planned how ARP timing and CAM learning will affect end-user disruption during a failover? fullNarratorScript:
In enterprise networks, the default gateway is the first hop every host uses to reach destinations outside its subnet. If that gateway device fails, many users instantly lose connectivity. This lesson introduces first hop redundancy protocols, or FHRPs, which present a virtual IP and virtual MAC so hosts can keep sending traffic even if a physical router goes offline. We'll focus on Cisco's HSRP and GLBP, and the open-standard VRRP. You'll learn the difference between active versus standby roles, how virtual MACs enable seamless failover, and when true load balancing with GLBP is preferable to simple redundancy. We'll also cover operational controls like preemption, priority, tracking, and authentication so your redundancy behaves predictably and securely. For example, with HSRP you can let the highest-priority switch be active, but use tracking to lower its priority if an uplink fails so traffic doesn't get blackholed. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to configure and verify HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP on Layer 3 switches and interpret their states with show commands. Consider how your campus or data center could benefit when a single device failure no longer disrupts user traffic.

By the end of this chapter you will understand why FHRPs are essential and how to operate three protocols used for first-hop resilience. First, you will be able to explain the necessity of a virtual IP and virtual MAC in preventing a single point of failure and give an example where an access switch host keeps routing during a gateway failure. Second, you will configure and verify HSRP for active/standby use, and create multiple HSRP groups for basic load distribution; this matters because many campus designs use HSRP on Layer 3 switches for VLAN gateways. Third, you will configure VRRP as the open-standard alternative and describe where VRRP’s behavior differs from HSRP; this is important in multi-vendor environments. Fourth, you will set up GLBP to deliver true per-packet or per-host load balancing using AVG and AVF roles, and use tracking and authentication to make failover graceful and secure. Each objective includes practical commands and verification so you can apply the skills in a lab or production environment.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on verification, troubleshooting, and a lab scenario. You will practice the key show and debug commands used to inspect FHRP state, including show standby brief for HSRP, show vrrp brief for VRRP, and show glbp brief for GLBP. These commands surface group numbers, roles, priorities, and virtual MACs so you can confirm correct operation. You will also learn to interpret hello timers and recognize when preemption or tracking is preventing an expected role change. Troubleshooting practice covers using debug messages cautiously to observe hellos and flaps when safe in a lab. Finally, you will apply these skills in a two-switch lab: configure HSRP on VLAN 10 with tracking on the uplink, and GLBP on VLAN 20 for load balancing. The ability to verify and diagnose with the right commands is as important as configuration—correct interpretation prevents disruptive changes in production.

First hop redundancy protocols create a shared gateway identity that hosts use as their default route. The shared identity consists of a virtual IP and usually a virtual MAC. Hosts ARP for the default gateway IP and receive a single MAC that corresponds to the protocol's virtual address. The key benefit is that host configurations remain static; endpoints do not need to know which physical router is active, and traffic continues to flow if a router fails. For example, an office workstation pointing at 192.168.10.1 continues to reach the internet when the physical switch that was forwarding traffic goes offline because a standby router assumes the virtual identity. A common misconception is that FHRPs make the network magically multipath; they provide gateway availability and, in GLBP's case, load distribution, but they do not replace proper bandwidth planning. Another point is that the virtual MAC is the control point for forwarding: if the MAC maps to a new physical device, frames follow. Remember that while HSRP and VRRP present a single virtual MAC for the group, GLBP assigns multiple virtual MACs so different hosts map to different physical forwarders. Think about how ARP caching on hosts and switch CAM behavior will affect failover timing and transient forwarding. How would you explain this behavior to an endpoint team concerned about ARP cache timeouts?

HSRP is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that elects one router to be Active and another to be Standby while the remaining routers listen. The Active router forwards traffic sent to the virtual IP and responds to ARP requests for the virtual MAC. Standby monitors the Active router using hello messages and will take over if the Active stops sending them. Other routers remain in the Listen state and do not forward for the virtual gateway. Election uses configured priority values; the highest priority becomes Active. If priorities match, the router with the higher IP address wins. Configuration typically uses standby group commands on the interface level to set the virtual IP, priority, and optionally enable preemption. A common pitfall is forgetting preempt: if a higher-priority router reboots and comes back online, without preempt it will not reclaim Active status and the network may continue using the lower-priority forwarder. Another practical consideration is ARP cache timing—after failover, host ARP entries may still reference an earlier MAC until they expire or refresh. In designs that require load sharing across VLANs, multiple HSRP groups can be used so different routers are Active for different subnets. Think about how you'll combine HSRP groups and tracking so a router with a failed uplink loses Active status for all relevant groups.

Let's walk through configuring HSRP on a VLAN interface and how to verify its operation. On an interface you define the virtual IP with standby group commands, set a priority, and enable preemption if you want a higher-priority device to reclaim Active after it recovers. For instance, setting standby 1 ip 192.168.10.1 and standby 1 priority 150 on SW1 configures the group. You also enable standby 1 preempt so SW1 will become Active again after reboot. To verify, run show standby brief to view the group's Active state, Virtual IP, and active MAC. A useful troubleshooting step is to purposely shut an uplink and confirm the standby becomes active, then bring the uplink back and ensure preemption behaves as expected. One misconception to avoid is believing that preempt alone guarantees immediate takeover; tracking can lower effective priority so preempt will not take effect if the calculated priority is lower. When you configure HSRP at scale, document group numbers per VLAN so you can plan load distribution. Practice these commands in the lab and use show standby and interface status to correlate physical and logical states.

Controlling who becomes Active is essential for predictable forwarding. Priority values determine election: higher priority wins. Preemption is a flag that permits a device with a higher priority, once it recovers, to take back the Active role. Tracking lets you tie effective priority to the state of an interface or object. For example, you can configure standby 1 track GigabitEthernet1/0/24 decrement 60. If that uplink goes down, the router reduces its effective priority by 60. If the resulting effective priority falls below the standby partner, the partner will become Active. Tracking avoids a situation where a router with a failed upstream path remains Active and blackholes traffic. A common misconception is thinking preempt overrides tracking; it does not. If a tracked interface remains down, the calculated priority might be lower so the higher-priority router will not preempt. In practice, plan your decrement values carefully so that a tracked failure reliably forces failover, but temporary blips don’t cause oscillation. Test by bringing the tracked interface down and observing show standby brief to confirm how the effective priority changed and which router became Active.

VRRP is the open-standard counterpart to HSRP and maps closely to the same concepts: a Master router forwards traffic for a virtual IP while Backup routers monitor and take over if the Master fails. Configuration uses vrrp group commands to set the virtual IP, priority, and optionally preempt. A key difference is that VRRP allows the virtual IP to be the actual IP address of the Master interface in some configurations, simplifying address management in mixed-vendor environments. Because VRRP is standardized in RFC 5798, it’s preferred when routers from different vendors must participate in gateway redundancy. Operationally, hello and hold timers work the same way in principle, and tracking and authentication are available similarly. An important misconception to avoid is assuming VRRP and HSRP are interchangeable without attention to subtle defaults like timers and authentication commands; when mixing vendors, confirm those settings match. When designing redundancy, choose VRRP when you need cross-vendor support and HSRP when you require Cisco-specific features or operational familiarity. Always verify with show vrrp brief to confirm Master selection and virtual MAC assignment. GLBP differs from HSRP and VRRP by allowing multiple physical routers to actively forward traffic for the same virtual IP. The protocol elects an Active Virtual Gateway, or AVG, which assigns unique virtual MACs to each Active Virtual Forwarder, or AVF. When a host ARPs for the virtual IP, the AVG replies with one of the AVF's virtual MAC addresses, often in round-robin order. That causes different hosts to have different MAC-to-physical-router mappings and distributes the forwarding load. GLBP supports multiple load-balancing methods: round-robin, host-dependent, and weighted. Round-robin cycles ARP responses among AVFs. Weighted allows AVFs to receive ARP responses proportional to their weight, useful if routers have asymmetric capacity. One misconception is assuming GLBP provides per-packet distribution; GLBP's distribution happens at ARP resolution time, so flows from the same host usually stick to a single AVF. When designing with GLBP, set priorities and weights thoughtfully and use show glbp brief to verify AVG, AVF roles, and virtual MAC assignments. GLBP is well-suited for environments where you want all gateway devices to share forwarding load without configuring multiple groups per VLAN.

Configuring GLBP starts with defining the GLBP group and virtual IP on the interface using glbp ip. Next set priorities and preemption as needed and choose a load-balancing method: round-robin, host-dependent, or weighted. Round-robin rotates ARP responses among AVFs and is the simplest default. Weighted lets you assign relative weights so higher-capacity routers receive ARP responses more often. For example, glbp 20 load-balancing round-robin configures the default behavior. Verification uses show glbp brief to confirm which router is AVG, which are AVFs, and the virtual MAC addresses assigned. Keep in mind GLBP gives per-host distribution at ARP resolution; it does not change the fact that each host typically sends all its traffic to one AVF until ARP changes. A common design choice is to use GLBP in VLANs where many hosts need to be balanced across distribution switches for capacity reasons. Avoid expecting instantaneous rebalancing when a device goes down—GLBP relies on ARP and may require ARP refresh to move hosts to remaining AVFs. Tracking and authentication are essential operational features for reliable and secure FHRP behavior. Tracking lets a router reduce its effective priority when a monitored object, typically an interface, goes down. You configure tracking with standby track [decrement ] for HSRP or vrrp track [decrement ] for VRRP and GLBP tracking syntax. The tracked decrement ensures that a router with a failed uplink does not become or remain Active, preventing traffic black-holing. Authentication prevents unauthorized devices from joining and impersonating the virtual gateway. For HSRP, you can configure MD5 authentication using standby authentication md5 key-string. Authentication prevents rogue devices from taking over by validating hellos. A common operational mistake is mismatched authentication parameters between peers, which prevents group formation. Another is setting too-large decrements that force unnecessary failovers for short-lived glitches. In your designs, balance sensitivity with stability: pick decrements that reflect real service loss and match authentication across peers. Regularly verify tracked objects and test the behavior in a lab before deploying to production. Troubleshooting FHRPs requires careful observation of show command output and conservative use of debug. Start with show standby brief, show vrrp brief, and show glbp brief to inspect group numbers, roles, effective priorities, virtual IPs, and virtual MACs. Compare these outputs across peers to confirm consistent virtual IP usage and matching authentication. If a group fails to form, look for mismatched timers, authentication keys, or incorrect interface bindings. Use interface show commands to verify IP addresses and whether the interface is up. If further detail is necessary, use debug standby or debug vrrp sparingly in a lab or maintenance window, because debug can affect device performance. Observing hellos can reveal why a router is not receiving or not sending messages. For GLBP-specific troubleshooting, confirm the AVG and AVF assignments and check weights when using weighted mode. A common root cause is an uplink or route problem, not the FHRP itself; tracking is intended to mitigate that risk by lowering priority when upstream paths fail. When diagnosing, correlate control-plane messages with data-plane symptoms and avoid making configuration changes blindly—document the current state, test in a lab, and then apply fixes during a maintenance window when possible.

When deploying FHRPs across a campus or data center, follow a few practical patterns to ensure stability and predictability. Use clear group numbering conventions per VLAN so you can plan which device is Active for which subnet without guesswork. For HSRP, assign higher priorities to devices with stronger uplinks and enable preempt only when you are confident tracked objects reflect production readiness. Use tracking to cause a router to step down when its upstream path fails. For GLBP, pick load-balancing methods that match application behavior: round-robin for broad distribution, weighted when routers have different capacity, and host-dependent when session affinity matters. Avoid overusing multiple groups across many VLANs to simulate load balancing; GLBP can be simpler where supported. Common mistakes include mismatched authentication, forgetting preempt where expected, inappropriate decrement magnitudes causing flapping, and assuming immediate rebalancing when an AVF fails. Let's summarize the essential concepts you should remember. First, FHRPs present a virtual IP and MAC to hosts so gateway availability is preserved across router outages. Second, HSRP is Cisco-proprietary and uses Active and Standby roles; you configure group numbers, virtual IPs, priority, and preempt to control behavior. Third, VRRP is an open standard providing Master and Backup roles and is preferred for multi-vendor environments. Fourth, GLBP provides true gateway load sharing by having an AVG assign virtual MACs to AVFs and responding to ARP with different MACs to distribute hosts. Lastly, operational features like tracking and authentication are crucial for graceful failover and security. As you work in labs and production, use show standby brief, show vrrp brief, and show glbp brief to verify state, and be careful with debug usage.
